A large square comprises a yellow square, two congruent blue rectangles, and a red square.


The yellow square has an area of 441 little squares. The two blue rectangles have a combined area of 1260 little squares.

What is the area, in little squares, of the red square?

Find the edge length of the yellow square by using the square-root operator.

\[x=\sqrt{441}\]

\[x=21\]

Find the area of each blue rectangle.

\[B=\frac{1260}{2}\] \[B=630\]

Each blue rectangle has one length of 21 and another of length \(y\).

\[xy~=~630\] \[21y~=~630\] \[y~=~30\]

The red square has side lengths equal to \(y=30\). To find its area, square the side length.

\[R=y^2\] \[R=30^2\] \[R=900\]

The area of the red square is 900 little squares.

A wrap-around L-shaped patio will measure 29 feet along both walls. The patio will stick out \(x\) feet from the walls, and the total area will be 759 square feet. Note: you can assume all angles are right angles.


What value of \(x\) satisfies the conditions stated above?

We can write an equation by saying the sum of \(x^2\) and \(29x\) and \(29x\) equals 759. These expressions represent the areas of a small square and two rectangles.


\[x^2+29x+29x~=~759\]

Combine like terms.

\[x^2+58x~=~759\]

There is a fun way to solve this. We will "complete the square". In this situation, the means we can imagine adding some extra area to the picture to make a large square. In this case, we need to add a square with edge lengths of 29, adding 841 square feet to the area.


\[x^2+58x+841~=~759+841\]

\[x^2+58x+841~=~1600\]

But, notice, if you look at the last picture, we have another way to represent the total area. The newly formed large square has side lengths of \(x+29\). So we can represent the total area of the large square as \((x+29)^2\).

\[(x+29)^2~=~1600\]

We can now use the square-root operation on both sides of the equation.

\[\sqrt{(x+29)^2}~=~\sqrt{1600}\]

\[x+29~=~40\]

And, lastly, subtract 29 from both sides of the equation.

\[x~=~40-29\]

\[x~=~11\]

We can write an equation by saying the sum of \(x^2\) and \(19x\) and \(19x\) equals 1008. These expressions represent the areas of a small square and two rectangles.


\[x^2+19x+19x~=~1008\]

Combine like terms.

\[x^2+38x~=~1008\]

There is a fun way to solve this. We will "complete the square". In this situation, the means we can imagine adding some extra area to the picture to make a large square. In this case, we need to add a square with edge lengths of 19, adding 361 square feet to the area.


\[x^2+38x+361~=~1008+361\]

\[x^2+38x+361~=~1369\]

But, notice, if you look at the last picture, we have another way to represent the total area. The newly formed large square has side lengths of \(x+19\). So we can represent the total area of the large square as \((x+19)^2\).

\[(x+19)^2~=~1369\]

We can now use the square-root operation on both sides of the equation.

\[\sqrt{(x+19)^2}~=~\sqrt{1369}\]

\[x+19~=~37\]

And, lastly, subtract 19 from both sides of the equation.

\[x~=~37-19\]

\[x~=~18\]

\[x~=~\pm12+8\]

\[x~=~15~~~~~~~~\text{or}~~~~~~~~x~=~-3\]

By completing the square, find both solutions to the given equation:

\[x^2-12x~=~-27\]

The given equation:

\[x^2-12x~=~-27\]

In order to make the left side of the equation a perfect square, we can add \(\left(\frac{-12}{2}\right)^2=36\) to both sides (where -12 is the linear coefficient).

\[x^2-12x+36~=~-27+36\]

\[x^2-12x+36~=~9\]

We can rewrite the left side in factored form. Notice that because the left side is a perfect square, we get a squared binomial.

\[(x-6)^2~=~9\]

Because the squaring function is not one-to-one, when we "undo" it in algebra, we need to consider the possibility of multiple solutions. In this case both 3 and -3 produce 9 when squared.

\[x-6~=~\pm 3\]

And, lastly, subtract -6 from both sides of the equation.

\[x~=~\pm3+6\]

\[x~=~9~~~~~~~~\text{or}~~~~~~~~x~=~3\]

\[x^2-8x~=~-7\]

\[x^2-8x~=~-7\]

In order to make the left side of the equation a perfect square, we can add \(\left(\frac{-8}{2}\right)^2=16\) to both sides (where -8 is the linear coefficient).

\[x^2-8x+16~=~-7+16\]

\[x^2-8x+16~=~9\]

We can rewrite the left side in factored form. Notice that because the left side is a perfect square, we get a squared binomial.

\[(x-4)^2~=~9\]

Because the squaring function is not one-to-one, when we "undo" it in algebra, we need to consider the possibility of multiple solutions. In this case both 3 and -3 produce 9 when squared.

\[x-4~=~\pm 3\]

And, lastly, subtract -4 from both sides of the equation.

\[x~=~\pm3+4\]

\[x~=~7~~~~~~~~\text{or}~~~~~~~~x~=~1\]
